title: How the Summa works
hook: objections first, then on the contrary, then I answer that, then replies

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy in the tower: Thomas, shut in by his own family, came out still a Dominican. Your line was he kept his call. What pulled at your yes, and what kept it? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

It seems that God does not exist. That sentence sits in the Summa Theologiae of Thomas Aquinas, a friar and a saint who gave his life to God. He wrote it himself, on purpose. Then he gave the reasons someone might say it. If God were infinite goodness, there would be no evil, and there is evil. And nature seems able to explain itself without any God at all. He set out the case against his own faith, plainly, before saying one word in reply. That isn't a slip. That's the method, and it runs through the book, article after article. Today's word is the book built that way.
screen: `IT SEEMS THAT GOD DOES NOT EXIST.` → `WRITTEN BY A SAINT.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The Summa Theologiae is Thomas's great book of theology, and in its opening lines he says who it's for: beginners. So it's built to be followed, one small step at a time. The book is cut into questions, and each question into articles. Every article asks one thing, as a yes or no. Whether God exists. Whether God is good. And every article moves the same way. First, the objections. Each one opens, it seems that, and gives the strongest reasons for the answer Thomas will not finally take. He doesn't hand the other side a weak case. He states it the way its friends would. Second, on the contrary. Usually a single short line from a voice the Church trusts, often Scripture, sometimes an earlier teacher like Augustine. It's a signal: there's another side to weigh. Third, I answer that. Now Thomas speaks for himself, and gives his reasons, in order. This is the heart of the article. Fourth, the replies. He goes back to the objections, one by one, and answers each. Often he grants what's true in an objection before showing where it goes wrong. Nothing raised at the start is left hanging at the end. Some readers hear in all this the debates of the medieval schools, written down. But step back and notice what the shape asks of the writer. You can't answer an objection you've never really heard. To reply to the other side, you first have to say it well enough that the person who holds it would say, yes, that's what I mean. Scripture gives the reason in the first letter of Peter, in the Douay-Rheims: "being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you." Ready, and listening first.
screen: `OBJECTIONS: IT SEEMS THAT…` · `ON THE CONTRARY` · `I ANSWER THAT` · `REPLIES, ONE BY ONE` · then, large: `A REASON OF THAT HOPE WHICH IS IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: state someone's objection fairly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a person who disagrees with you about something that matters. Faith, politics, how to raise a child, anything. Now say their view, silently, the way Thomas would: it seems that. Give their best reason, then their second. Use the words they would use, not the ones you'd use to tease them. Keep going until you think they would nod. Don't answer it. Not yet. Just let their side stand there, stated well. If you pray, you can hold that person before God for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Summa. Thomas Aquinas's great book of theology, built of questions and articles, each one moving from objections, to on the contrary, to I answer that, to replies. Today's word.
Your line: state the other side first. Today, before you argue with anyone, say their point back to them, and ask if you got it right. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Catholic seminaries and universities often teach students to read an article of the Summa in its four moves, objections, on the contrary, I answer that, and replies, and some use the same shape for classroom debates.

fork.setup: you're writing a book about God for beginners. you reach the question, does God exist? what do you write first?
options: your own answer, as clearly as you can.
the strongest reasons someone might say no.
fork.reveal: Thomas opens with the objections: it seems that God does not exist, and why. Scripture comes next, then his answer, then a reply to each objection.

original.note: Latin: I answer that it must be said — the words that open Thomas's own answer in each article.

trapdoor: what you thought: a giant summary of Catholic answers.
what it means: a book that asks one question at a time, states the other side first, answers, then replies to each objection.
what a scholar hears: videtur quod, sed contra, respondeo, ad primum: the same four moves, article after article, written for beginners.

notes: 'It seems that God does not exist' and the four headings follow the English Dominican Province translation (1920s), which is public domain in the US but not on the validator's list, so they are spoken without quotation marks and cited as paraphrase.
Prologue: Thomas says the work is for the instruction of beginners (incipientium). Confirm the paraphrase.
The two objections in I.2.3 (evil; nature explains itself) are summarized, not quoted.
'Some readers hear the debates of the medieval schools' (the disputed question) is offered as a reading, not a historical claim; confirm or cut.
Original: 'respondeo dicendum' glossed as 'I answer that it must be said'; confirm pronunciation (ecclesiastical Latin).
